claim: Biomedical single-cell atlases describe disease at the cellular level.
source: Biomedical single-cell atlases describe disease at the cellular level.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of single-cell atlases presented in the abstract.

claim: Analysis of single-cell data commonly focuses on cell-type-centric pairwise cross-condition comparisons, disregarding the multicellular nature of disease processes.
source: However, analysis of this data commonly focuses on cell-type-centric pairwise cross-condition comparisons, disregarding the multicellular nature of disease processes.
evidence: This statement describes current limitations in single-cell data analysis approaches.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis repurposes group factor analysis as implemented in multi-omics factor analysis.
source: Here, we propose multicellular factor analysis for the unsupervised analysis of samples from cross-condition single-cell atlases and the identification of multicellular programs associated with disease. Our strategy, which repurposes group factor analysis as implemented in multi-omics factor analysis
evidence: The authors explicitly state their methodological approach.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis incorporates the variation of patient samples across cell-types or other tissue-centric features.
source: Our strategy, which repurposes group factor analysis as implemented in multi-omics factor analysis, incorporates the variation of patient samples across cell-types or other tissue-centric features, such as cell compositions or spatial relationships
evidence: The authors describe the capabilities of their proposed method.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis enables the joint analysis of multiple patient cohorts, facilitating the integration of atlases.
source: incorporates the variation of patient samples across cell-types or other tissue-centric features, such as cell compositions or spatial relationships, and enables the joint analysis of multiple patient cohorts, facilitating the integration of atlases.
evidence: The authors state a key capability of their method.

claim: The framework was applied to a collection of acute and chronic human heart failure atlases.
source: We applied our framework to a collection of acute and chronic human heart failure atlases
evidence: The authors describe their application of the method.

claim: Multicellular processes of cardiac remodeling were described that were independent to cellular compositions and their local organization.
source: We applied our framework to a collection of acute and chronic human heart failure atlases and described multicellular processes of cardiac remodeling, independent to cellular compositions and their local organization
evidence: The authors report findings from their analysis.

claim: The multicellular processes of cardiac remodeling were conserved in independent spatial and bulk transcriptomics datasets.
source: described multicellular processes of cardiac remodeling, independent to cellular compositions and their local organization, that were conserved in independent spatial and bulk transcriptomics datasets.
evidence: The authors report validation of their findings across different data modalities.

claim: The availability of cross-condition single-cell transcriptomics atlases profiling the pathological state of different tissues and organs in humans has increased during the last years.
source: The availability of cross-condition single-cell transcriptomics atlases profiling the pathological state of different tissues and organs in humans has increased during the last years and will continue to expand in different areas of the biomedical field (Rood et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rood et al., 2022.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis is usually performed to compare the molecular profiles of cell types across groups of samples over distinct conditions.
source: Differential gene expression analysis is usually performed for this task, in which the gene expression of each cell type is contrasted across various conditions (Crowell et al., 2020; Squair et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement describes a common analytical approach and is supported by citations.

claim: The cell-type-centric approach treats each cell-type-specific alteration in disease independently from each other, ignoring particular gene expression changes of one cell type that may relate to the changes of other cell types.
source: This cell-type-centric approach treats each cell-type-specific alteration in disease independently from each other, ignoring particular gene expression changes of one cell type that may relate to the changes of other cell types, here referred to as multicellular programs.
evidence: The authors identify a limitation of current approaches.

claim: Cell-type-centric approaches require a specific definition of cross-condition contrasts a priori.
source: Another limitation of these approaches is that they require a specific definition of cross-condition contrasts a priori.
evidence: The authors identify another limitation of current approaches.

claim: Novel tissue-centric computational methods for multicellular integration have emerged that are helpful in the definition of multicellular programs associated with clinical covariates of interest.
source: A set of novel tissue-centric computational methods for multicellular integration have emerged that are helpful in the definition of multicellular programs associated with clinical covariates of interest (Jerby-Arnon and Regev, 2022), and the unsupervised analysis of samples from cross-condition single-cell atlases (Armingol et al., 2022; Mitchel et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant methods.

claim: Multicellular integration methods are extensions of matrix factorization that aim to reduce the dimensionality of the data while retaining most of the variability.
source: These multicellular integration methods are extensions of matrix factorization that aim to reduce the dimensionality of the data while retaining most of the variability.
evidence: The authors describe the technical nature of these methods.

claim: Multicellular integration methods first transform cross-condition single-cell data into a multi-view representation, in which each view contains the summarized gene expression profile across cells of the same type for each sample.
source: A key element of multicellular integration methods is that they first transform cross-condition single-cell data into a multi-view representation, in which each view contains the summarized gene expression profile across cells of the same type for each sample.
evidence: The authors describe how these methods process data.

claim: In multicellular integration the objective is to measure the variability of samples across multiple cell types simultaneously.
source: in multicellular integration the objective is to measure the variability of samples (e.g. patient tissues) across multiple cell types simultaneously.
evidence: The authors define the objective of multicellular integration.

claim: No current framework has been proposed to map multicellular programs to other complementary data types such as spatial and bulk omics.
source: Although existing multicellular integration methods can capture coordinated gene expression events across cell types associated with disease from single-cell data, no current framework has been proposed to map these multicellular programs to other complementary data types such as spatial and bulk omics.
evidence: The authors identify a gap in current methods.

claim: Spatial data could be used to understand the spatial regulation of multicellular alterations in disease.
source: Spatial data could be used to understand the spatial regulation of multicellular alterations in disease.
evidence: The authors propose a potential application of spatial data.

claim: Multicellular programs could be used to deconvolute cell-type-specific gene expression alterations in disease from bulk transcriptomics data.
source: Moreover, multicellular programs could be used to deconvolute cell-type-specific gene expression alterations in disease from bulk transcriptomics data, complementing current cell-type deconvolution methods that only estimate cell-type compositions of tissues (Avila Cobos et al., 2020).
evidence: The authors propose a potential application and cite existing deconvolution methods.

claim: Group factor analysis as implemented in MOFA can be repurposed to perform and extend similar tissue-centric analyses as the ones performed by multicellular integration methods.
source: Here, we show that group factor analysis as implemented in multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) (Argelaguet et al., 2020; Argelaguet et al., 2018), can be repurposed in a straightforward manner to perform and extend similar tissue-centric analyses as the ones performed by multicellular integration methods
evidence: The authors state their main methodological contribution with citations to MOFA.

claim: MOFA uses similar multi-view data representations and model objectives to create latent spaces as multicellular integration methods.
source: can be repurposed in a straightforward manner to perform and extend similar tissue-centric analyses as the ones performed by multicellular integration methods, since it uses similar multi-view data representations and model objectives to create latent spaces.
evidence: The authors explain why MOFA is suitable for their purpose.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis overcomes the limitation of data completeness that some multicellular integration methods enforce.
source: Benefiting from the flexibility of the statistical framework of MOFA, multicellular factor analysis overcomes the limitation of data completeness that some multicellular integration methods enforce (Armingol et al., 2022; Mitchel et al., 2022), where all samples must contain information in all cell-type views and all cell-type views must contain the same features.
evidence: The authors identify an advantage of their method over existing methods with citations.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis provides the unique possibility of jointly analyzing samples of independent studies allowing for meta-analysis.
source: In contrast to the aforementioned methods, multicellular factor analysis also provides the unique possibility of jointly analyzing samples of independent studies allowing for meta-analysis.
evidence: The authors claim a unique capability of their method.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis is capable of modeling various classes of tissue-centric views including cell-type compositional data, spatial organization patterns, or communication inference scores.
source: Moreover, multicellular factor analysis is capable of modeling various classes of tissue-centric views including cell-type compositional data, spatial organization patterns, or communication inference scores, generalizing the framework of available methods that only model one class of tissue-level views (i.e. gene expression across cell types).
evidence: The authors describe the versatility of their method.

claim: The acute heart failure atlas contained 27 left ventricle heart single nuclei samples of three tissue conditions across seven cell types.
source: After quality control, this dataset contained 27 left ventricle heart single nuclei samples of three tissue conditions across seven cell types previously annotated: myogenic (n=13), fibrotic (n=5), and ischemic (n=9) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The authors describe the dataset composition.

claim: The seven cell types in the acute heart failure atlas included cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle, endothelial, myeloid, and lymphoid cells.
source: The seven cell types, previously profiled and annotated across samples, included cardiomyocytes (CMs), fibroblasts (Fibs), pericytes (PCs), and vascular smooth muscle (vSMCs), endothelial (Endos), myeloid, and lymphoid cells.
evidence: The authors list the cell types analyzed.

claim: The latent space returned by the multicellular factor analysis model fitted to the single-cell atlas explained on average 63.8% of the variability of gene expression of the genes across cell types.
source: The latent space returned by the multicellular factor analysis model fitted to the single-cell atlas (Figure 2A) explained on average 63.8% of the variability of gene expression of the genes across cell types.
evidence: The authors report a quantitative result from their analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the samples based on their six factor scores effectively separated ischemic, fibrotic, and myogenic-enriched samples.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the samples based on their six factor scores effectively separated ischemic, fibrotic, and myogenic-enriched samples.
evidence: The authors report a result from their clustering analysis.

claim: From the six recovered factors, Factor 1, 2, and 6 were associated with the previously defined tissue condition labels.
source: From the six recovered factors, Factor 1, 2, and 6 were associated with the previously defined tissue condition labels (Kruskall-Wallis test adj. p-value <0.05, mean percentage of explained variance across cell types of 52.2%, Figure 2A and C)
evidence: The authors report statistical associations with supporting p-values.

claim: Factors 2 and 4 were associated with the technical label.
source: and Factors 2 and 4 were associated with the technical label (Kruskall-Wallis test adj. p-value <0.05, mean percentage of explained variance across cell types of 14.7%, Figure 2D).
evidence: The authors report statistical associations with supporting p-values.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis can be applied to cross-condition single-cell atlases for exploratory unsupervised analysis that enables the detection and prioritization of biological signals.
source: Our results suggest that multicellular factor analysis can be applied to cross-condition single-cell atlases for exploratory unsupervised analysis that enables the detection and prioritization of biological signals.
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion from their results.

claim: scITD could only analyze 24 of the 27 samples given the data completeness constraints of their statistical framework based on tensor decomposition.
source: First, we observed that compared to multicellular factor analysis, scITD could only analyze 24 of the 27 samples given the data completeness constraints of their statistical framework based on tensor decomposition.
evidence: The authors report a limitation of the comparison method.

claim: Silhouette scores were comparable across methods for all of the biological and technical labels, except for myogenic-enriched samples which were more similar to each other in the multicellular factor analysis's latent space.
source: Silhouette scores were comparable across methods for all of the biological and technical labels, except for myogenic-enriched samples which were more similar to each other in the multicellular factor analysis's latent space (Wilcoxon test, adj. p-value <0.01, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The authors report a comparative result with statistical support.

claim: Multicellular factor analysis allows for a more flexible definition of cell-type views that better handles missing information and possible technical biases, such as background gene expression.
source: However, compared to scITD's framework, multicellular factor analysis allows for a more flexible definition of cell-type views that better handles missing information and possible technical biases, such as background gene expression.
evidence: The authors conclude an advantage of their method based on their analysis.

claim: A MOFA model with four factors explained on average 59% of gene expression variability across cell types in the lupus dataset.
source: A model of four factors explained on average 59% of gene expression variability across cell types.
evidence: The authors report a quantitative result from their analysis of the lupus dataset.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of all factor scores grouped separately stimulated from non-stimulated samples in the lupus dataset.
source: Hierarchical clustering of all factor scores grouped separately stimulated from non-stimulated samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The authors report a result from clustering analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Factor 1 in the lupus dataset was associated with IFN-beta stimulation and explained on average 50.9% of the variability of gene expression across cell types.
source: Factor 1, associated with IFN-beta stimulation (Kruskall-Wallis test adj. p-value <0.05), explained on average 50.9% of the variability of gene expression across cell types
evidence: The authors report statistical associations and quantitative results.

claim: CD14+ monocytes, FCGR3A+ monocytes, and dendritic cells had the largest explained variance (>60%) in the lupus dataset, suggesting that these cells may be the most responsive to the stimulation.
source: being CD14+ monocytes, FCGR3A+ monocytes, and dendritic cells, the cells with the largest explained variance (>60%), suggesting that these cells may be the most responsive to the stimulation.
evidence: The authors report data and make an inference about cell responsiveness.

claim: From the collection of 3136 unique highly variable genes used in the model across cell types, the median number of genes associated with Factor 1 per cell type was 322.
source: First, from the collection of 3136 unique highly variable genes used in the model across cell types, we observed that after filtering by importance (gene weight in Factor 1 different from 0), the median number of genes associated with Factor 1 per cell type was 322 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from their gene analysis.

claim: 12% of the genes associated with Factor 1 were relevant for more than a single cell type.
source: Additionally, 12% of the genes associated with Factor 1 were relevant for more than a single cell type, suggesting that the multicellular coordinated gene expression associated with myocardial remodeling captured by multicellular factor analysis is mainly dominated by cell-type-specific processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The authors report a quantitative result and make an inference.

claim: Cell-type myogenic signatures (median size across cell types=243) were larger than the ischemic ones (median size across cell types=76).
source: We observed that cell-type myogenic signatures (median size across cell types=243) were larger than the ischemic ones (median size across cell types=76), indicating a general trend of downregulation of gene expression of the cells in the myocardium after ischemic injury (Figure 3B).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results and make an inference about gene expression trends.

claim: There was little overlap between myogenic and ischemic cell-type factor gene signatures across cell types (Jaccard index of 0.06 and 0.04, for ischemic and myogenic signatures, respectively).
source: Additionally, we observed little overlap between myogenic and ischemic cell-type factor gene signatures across cell types (Jaccard index of 0.06 and 0.04, for ischemic and myogenic signatures, respectively, Figure 3C).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from overlap analysis.

claim: The multicellular transcriptional alterations upon myocardial infarction captured by the model represent mostly cell-type-specific processes, with a small subset of general processes shared between cell types.
source: Altogether, our observations suggest that the multicellular transcriptional alterations upon myocardial infarction captured by the model represent mostly cell-type-specific processes, with a small subset of general processes shared between cell types.
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion from their observations.

claim: The median Pearson correlation between the factor gene weights and the log fold changes across cell types was the highest for the contrast between ischemic and myogenic samples (0.98).
source: The median Pearson correlation between the factor gene weights and the log fold changes across cell types was the highest for the contrast between ischemic and myogenic samples (0.98), followed by the contrast between ischemic and fibrotic samples (0.74), and the contrast between fibrotic and myogenic samples (0.65)
evidence: The authors report quantitative correlation results.

claim: Factor 1 captures the molecular changes associated with the progression of myocardial remodeling, where fibrotic samples represent an intermediary or pseudo-recovered state.
source: suggesting that Factor 1 captures the molecular changes associated with the progression of myocardial remodeling, where fibrotic samples represent an intermediary or pseudo-recovered state.
evidence: The authors make an inference based on correlation results.

claim: 77% of genes across cell types included in the multicellular program were differentially expressed (edgeR adj. p-value ≤ 0.05) in at least one contrast.
source: Moreover, we observed that from all genes across cell types included in the multicellular program, 77% of them were differentially expressed (edgeR adj. p-value ≤ 0.05) in at least one contrast.
evidence: The authors report a quantitative result from differential expression analysis.

claim: Ischemic signatures captured mainly a multicellular response to hypoxia and inflammation across the majority of the cells, together with enrichment of fibrotic processes and angiogenesis.
source: Enrichment of MSigDB's hallmarks (Liberzon et al., 2015) showed that ischemic signatures captured mainly a multicellular response to hypoxia and inflammation across the majority of the cells, together with enrichment of fibrotic processes and angiogenesis.
evidence: The authors report results from functional enrichment analysis with citation.

claim: Myogenic signatures were enriched by homeostatic oxidative phosphorylation processes in CMs and Fibs, together with specific processes of Endos regarding responses to interferons and TGFb activities.
source: Myogenic signatures were enriched by homeostatic oxidative phosphorylation processes in CMs and Fibs, together with specific processes of Endos regarding responses to interferons and TGFb activities.
evidence: The authors report results from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Myogenic cell-type factor signatures had an overrepresentation of marker genes of cell states that increased in abundance in myogenic samples, compared to ischemic and fibrotic ones.
source: We observed across cell types that myogenic cell-type factor signatures had an overrepresentation of marker genes of cell states that increased in abundance in myogenic samples, compared to ischemic and fibrotic ones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, hypergeometric test adj. p-value <0.05).
evidence: The authors report results from enrichment analysis with statistical support.

claim: Ischemic signatures were enriched by marker genes of cell states that increased in abundance in ischemic and fibrotic samples.
source: In contrast, ischemic signatures were enriched by marker genes of cell states that increased in abundance in ischemic and fibrotic samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, hypergeometric test adj. p-value <0.05).
evidence: The authors report results from enrichment analysis with statistical support.

claim: Cell-type-specific Factor 1 gene signatures captured transcriptional changes related to the change in compositions of functional cell states as a consequence of the disease context.
source: Overall, we showed that cell-type-specific Factor 1 gene signatures captured transcriptional changes related to the change in compositions of functional cell states as a consequence of the disease context.
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion from their cell state analysis.

claim: Across all cell-type-specific factor gene signatures, differentially expressed genes between conditions (ANOVA adj. p-value <0.01) were observed that were conserved across cell states.
source: Across all cell-type-specific factor gene signatures, we observed differentially expressed genes between conditions (ANOVA adj. p-value <0.01) that were conserved across cell states (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: The authors report results from statistical analysis with reference to figures.

claim: In general, across all cell-type signatures, a greater proportion of variance of gene expression was explained by the samples' condition, rather than the cell state.
source: We observed that in general, across all cell-type signatures, a greater proportion of variance of gene expression was explained by the samples' condition, rather than the cell state (one-sample-t-test adj. p-value <0.01, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: The authors report results from statistical analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The genes defining the multicellular latent variable associated with myocardial remodeling recovered by the model capture both cell-state-dependent and -independent transcriptional changes.
source: suggesting that the genes defining the multicellular latent variable associated with myocardial remodeling recovered by the model capture both cell-state-dependent and -independent transcriptional changes.
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion from their variance analysis.

claim: While certain cell states increase in their relative abundance during myocardial infarction, cells within a tissue and cell type partake in a shared global transcriptional response to injury.
source: Moreover, these results suggest that while certain cell states increase in their relative abundance during myocardial infarction, cells within a tissue and cell type partake in a shared global transcriptional response to injury, a novel observation not reported in the original manuscript of this data.
evidence: The authors make an inference and claim novelty of the finding.

claim: Across cell types, except for PCs and lymphoid cells, the expression of ischemic programs occur in larger areas and with a bigger magnitude in ischemic samples compared to myogenic samples.
source: As hypothesized, we observed that across cell types, except for PCs and lymphoid cells, the expression of ischemic programs occur in larger areas and with a bigger magnitude in ischemic samples compared to myogenic samples (Wilcoxon test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The authors report results from spatial analysis with statistical support.

claim: The expression of myogenic programs of Fibs and CMs was more abundant in myogenic samples compared to the ischemic ones.
source: Similarly, the expression of myogenic programs of Fibs and CMs was more abundant in myogenic samples compared to the ischemic ones (Wilcoxon test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The authors report results from spatial analysis with statistical support.

claim: Compared to myogenic tissues, fibrotic ones expressed ischemic programs of Fibs in larger areas, while their myogenic programs were expressed in smaller areas.
source: Compared to myogenic tissues, fibrotic ones expressed ischemic programs of Fibs in larger areas, while their myogenic programs were expressed in smaller areas (Wilcoxon test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The authors report results from spatial analysis with statistical support.

claim: The multicellular program associated with myocardial remodeling captured by multicellular factor analysis relates to the extent to which myogenic and ischemic cell-type programs are expressed in tissues.
source: Our analyses showed that the multicellular program associated with myocardial remodeling captured by multicellular factor analysis relates to the extent to which myogenic and ischemic cell-type programs are expressed in tissues.
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion from their spatial mapping analysis.

claim: The extended model incorporated four additional sample views describing compositions and spatial dependencies of cell types.
source: The extended model incorporated four additional sample views. The first of these new views described the compositions of the seven cell-types analyzed, and the other three views quantified the spatial dependencies between these seven cell types in three different spatial contexts estimated from ST: colocalization, local-neighborhood, and extended-neighborhood dependencies.
evidence: The authors describe the composition of their extended model.

claim: The latent space returned by the extended model explained on average 63.8% of the variability of gene expression of the genes across cell types.
source: The latent space returned by the extended model explained on average 63.8% of the variability of gene expression of the genes across cell types, showing that the extended model did not lose explanatory power of the molecular views of the tissue samples after adding the structural views since the performance was identical to the original model.
evidence: The authors report quantitative results and compare to the original model.

claim: The latent space of the extended model captured 70% of the variability in compositions of cell types of the analyzed tissues and on average 22.8% of the variability in spatial dependencies.
source: We observed that the latent space of the extended model captured 70% of the variability in compositions of cell types of the analyzed tissues and on average 22.8% of the variability in spatial dependencies.
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from the extended model.

claim: The low percentage of explained variance captured by the extended model of the spatial dependencies views might suggest that the variability in the spatial organization of cells in cardiac tissues cannot be mainly explained by the patient conditions.
source: The low percentage of explained variance captured by the extended model of the spatial dependencies views might suggest that the variability in the spatial organization of cells in cardiac tissues cannot be mainly explained by the patient conditions, and other variables such as the location of tissue sampling may dominate the signal of ST.
evidence: The authors make an inference from their quantitative results.

claim: Shared multicellular programs across samples of the same condition despite variable cellular organization suggests a degree of independence between the local organization of cells in cardiac tissues and their overall response to the ischemic context of myocardial infarction.
source: Moreover, the fact that we could identify shared multicellular programs across samples of the same condition despite variable cellular organization suggests a degree of independence between the local organization of cells in cardiac tissues and their overall response to the ischemic context of myocardial infarction.
evidence: The authors make an inference from their results.

claim: The first chronic heart failure study (Chaffin2022) encompassed 42 single nuclei cardiac samples profiling healthy myocardium (n=16) and end-stage heart failure both from dilated (n=11) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies (n=15).
source: The first study (Chaffin2022) encompassed 42 single nuclei cardiac samples profiling healthy myocardium (n=16) and end-stage heart failure both from dilated (n=11) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies (n=15) (Chaffin et al., 2022a).
evidence: The authors describe the dataset with citation.

claim: The second chronic heart failure study (Reichart2022) profiled 79 cardiac samples of healthy myocardium (n=18) together with samples of dilated (n=52), non-compaction (n=1), and arrhythmogenic right ventricular (n=8) cardiomyopathy.
source: The second study (Reichart2022) profiled 79 cardiac samples of healthy myocardium (n=18) together with samples of dilated (n=52), non-compaction (n=1), and arrhythmogenic right ventricular (n=8) cardiomyopathy (Reichart et al., 2022b).
evidence: The authors describe the dataset with citation.

claim: Baseline study-specific models captured a mean total amount of explained variance across cell types of 43% for both datasets.
source: Baseline study-specific models captured a mean total amount of explained variance across cell types of 43% for both datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from baseline models.

claim: A mean percentage of explained variance across cell types of 25% and 21% was associated with heart failure for Chaffin2022 and Reichart2022, respectively.
source: A mean percentage of explained variance across cell types of 25% and 21% was associated with heart failure for Chaffin2022 and Reichart2022, respectively (Kruskal-Wallis test adj p-value <0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results with statistical support.

claim: The area under the PRC of the classifier of Reichart2022's patients using Chaffin2022's factors was 0.69.
source: The area under the PRC of the classifier of Reichart2022's patients using Chaffin2022's factors was 0.69, and we observed a higher performance on the classification of Chaffin2022's patient samples using Reichart2022's factors with an area under the PRC of 0.87.
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from classification analysis.

claim: The multicellular programs inferred from Reichart2022 better generalize the description of heart failure in comparison to Chaffin2022, which could be explained by the higher degree of variance within the heart failure patients in the former study.
source: These results suggest that the multicellular programs inferred from Reichart2022 better generalize the description of heart failure in comparison to Chaffin2022, which could be explained by the higher degree of variance within the heart failure patients in the former study.
evidence: The authors make an inference from their classification results.

claim: In contrast to the study-specific models, the joint model had a reduction of mean total amount of explained variance across cell types of only 0.6% and 0.51% for Chaffin2022 and Reichart2022, respectively.
source: In contrast to the study-specific models, the joint model had a reduction of mean total amount of explained variance across cell types of only 0.6% and 0.51% for Chaffin2022 and Reichart2022, respectively, suggesting that joint modeling had no critical effects on the construction of the multicellular latent space.
evidence: The authors report quantitative results and make an inference.

claim: The joint model had an increased mean percentage of explained variance across cell types associated with heart failure of 4.9% for Chaffin2022 and 9.12% for Reichart2022.
source: The joint model had an increased mean percentage of explained variance across cell types associated with heart failure of 4.9% for Chaffin2022 and 9.12% for Reichart2022, supporting the idea that the inclusion of multiple studies could better define conserved disease signals.
evidence: The authors report quantitative results and make an inference.

claim: From the six factors reconstructed in the joint model, three factors associated with the patient conditions, from which two (Factors 1 and 2) discriminated failing and non-failing hearts in both studies.
source: From the six factors reconstructed in the joint model, three factors associated with the patient conditions, from which two (Factors 1 and 2) discriminated failing and non-failing hearts in both studies, and two factors (Factor 4) were only associated to the differences between conditions in Reichart2022's (Kruskal-Wallis test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 5B).
evidence: The authors report results from factor analysis with statistical support.

claim: Functional characterization of the cell-type-specific Factor 1 signatures revealed known multicellular processes active in failing hearts, such as the activation of JAK-STAT, TGFb, and WNT signaling pathways, related to inflammatory and fibrotic processes, together with the reactivation of fetal programs.
source: Functional characterization of the cell-type-specific Factor 1 signatures revealed known multicellular processes active in failing hearts, such as the activation of JAK-STAT, TGFb, and WNT signaling pathways, related to inflammatory and fibrotic processes, together with the reactivation of fetal programs (Liew and Dzau, 2004; Figure 5C).
evidence: The authors report results from functional characterization with citation.

claim: The identification of a shared multicellular program of cardiac remodeling associated with heart failure across studies and etiologies suggest the existence of a convergent multicellular functional molecular state of failing myocardium independent of the initial causes of heart failure and sampling variability.
source: Moreover, the identification of a shared multicellular program of cardiac remodeling associated with heart failure across studies and etiologies suggest the existence of a convergent multicellular functional molecular state of failing myocardium independent of the initial causes of heart failure and sampling variability.
evidence: The authors make an inference from their meta-analysis results.

claim: SCDC had the highest median Pearson correlation and the least median root-mean-squared error with the true compositions across studies (median Pearson correlation = 0.84, median root-mean-squared error = 0.108).
source: We observed that SCDC had the highest median Pearson correlation and the least median root-mean-squared error with the true compositions across studies (median Pearson correlation = 0.84, median root-mean-squared error = 0.108), thus we used this method for the deconvolution of ReHeaT's studies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The authors report quantitative results from method comparison.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of cell-type-specific signature scores across samples in ReHeaT showed a general conservation of the heart failure signature identified from single-cell data, in which bulk failing hearts had negative signature scores across cell types.
source: Hierarchical clustering of cell-type-specific signature scores across samples in ReHeaT showed a general conservation of the heart failure signature identified from single-cell data, in which bulk failing hearts had negative signature scores across cell types (Figure 5D, left).
evidence: The authors report results from clustering analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The conservation of the heart failure signal in bulk samples was independent of their estimated cell compositions.
source: We observed that the conservation of the heart failure signal in bulk samples was independent of their estimated cell compositions, since hierarchical clustering of cell-type compositions led to a greater mixing of failing and non-failing samples (Figure 5D, right), which was quantified using silhouette scores in only RNA-seq samples (Wilcoxon test, adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 5E).
evidence: The authors report results from clustering analysis with statistical support.

claim: In 9 of the 16 bulk studies, a congruent difference in the expression of at least one cell-type-specific factor signature between failing and non-failing hearts was observed.
source: In 9 of the 16 bulk studies, we observed a congruent difference in the expression of at least one cell-type-specific factor signature between failing and non-failing hearts (Wilcoxon test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The authors report results from statistical testing across multiple studies.

claim: In six of these studies we could differentiate failing and non-failing hearts using all of the cell-type-specific factor signatures except for lymphoid cells.
source: Additionally, in six of these studies we could differentiate failing and non-failing hearts using all of the cell-type-specific factor signatures except for lymphoid cells (Wilcoxon test adj. p-value <0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
